Use December 31, 2025 as the opening balance-sheet date and incorporate reported first-quarter 2026 results. Explain the economic basis for the forecast, reconcile its income-statement, cash-flow, and balance-sheet implications, and assess the principal uncertainty affecting the estimates.

Prediction intervals:
For each requested point forecast, also report the lower and upper endpoints of a central 80% prediction interval for that same realized metric, period, accounting basis and unit. The endpoints represent your 10th and 90th predictive percentiles, not a confidence interval for an estimated mean and not unlabeled optimistic/pessimistic cases. Endpoints must be finite and ordered. The point estimate need not be the midpoint; state its interpretation if needed. Explain a quantitative scenario or statistical basis for both endpoints and link the uncertainty to cutoff-valid financial drivers. A judgmental scenario distribution is allowed; an unweighted worst/best range alone does not establish 80% coverage. No particular model, sample count or backtest is required. Each interval is marginal: 80% for each metric does not claim 80% simultaneous coverage of all metrics. Explain the intervals in the same research report.

Accrual and joint-uncertainty consistency:
Use the standalone consolidated accrued-interest-payable balance, not a broader other-liabilities total. Establish the reported first-quarter opening/expense/cash-payment/closing bridge and count the observed first quarter exactly once in each six-month flow. Let B0 be December 31 payable, E the six-month interest expense and P the six-month cash interest paid. Reconcile June payable B as B=B0+E-P+J. Set J=0 unless a separately identified scope or noncash adjustment is justified by cutoff-valid evidence and explicit prospective assumptions; do not insert J merely to close a gap. State any such adjustment and its sign.
Describe a coherent joint scenario or probabilistic construction for E, P and B that respects this identity in each underlying state, including any justified J. Derive the three marginal intervals from that common construction and explain how funding-cost uncertainty differs from payment-timing uncertainty. A compact equation-based or scenario-based explanation with supported endpoint calculations is sufficient; no simulation dump or fixed number of scenarios is required. Do not claim that three marginal 80% intervals form a joint 80% region.

Submission:
Submit a complete research report with your conclusion, supporting analysis, relevant calculations and citations.

Management believes that, as of March 31, 2026, the Company meets all capital adequacy requirements to which it is subject.
Basel III became effective for the Company and its bank subsidiary on January 1, 2015. Basel III amended the prompt corrective action rules to incorporate a CET1 requirement and to raise the capital requirements for certain capital categories. In order to be adequately capitalized for purposes of the prompt corrective action rules, a banking organization is required to have at least a 4.5% CET1 risk-based capital ratio, a 4% Tier 1 leverage capital ratio, a 6% Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio and an 8% total risk-based capital ratio.
The Federal Reserve Board’s risk-based capital guidelines include the definitions for (1) a well-capitalized institution, (2) an adequately-capitalized institution, and (3) an undercapitalized institution. Under Basel III, the criteria for a well-capitalized institution are: a 6.5% CET1 risk-based capital ratio, a 5% Tier 1 leverage capital ratio, an 8% Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio, and a 10% total risk-based capital ratio. As of March 31, 2026, the Bank met the capital standards for a well-capitalized institution. The Company’s CET1 risk-based capital ratio, Tier 1 leverage capital ratio, Tier 1 risk-based capital ratio, and total risk-based capital ratio were 16.70%, 14.30%, 16.70%, and 19.46%, respectively, as of March 31, 2026.
